newsitem.title: INDIA: India pilots say government dragged feet on safety.
newsitem.headline: India pilots say government dragged feet on safety.

text.p: Indian pilots said on Wednesday the government had dragged its feet on improving flight safety standards after three near mid-air collisions over six months in 1994 and 1995.

The Indian Commercial Pilots' Association (ICPA) said the near misses, between October 1994 and April 1995, had highlighted a surge in air traffic in Indian skies following the opening up of the economy in 1991.
But it said the government had yet to respond fully to recommendations it made in mid-1995.
The world's worst mid-air collision on Tuesday between a Saudi Arabian Airlines jumbo and a Kazakh cargo plane turned the spotlight on India's safety standards.

There was no immediate explanation for the disaster, in which some 350 passengers died, but speculation ran from inadequate equipment at Delhi airport to pilot misunderstanding of ground controller instructions.
The ICPA said the need to upgrade flight safety equipment at airports became glaringly apparent after the near misses in 1994 and 1995.

The pilot's association released a letter dated May, 1995, saying a major mid-air collision was averted on October 16, 1994, when a Gulf Air flight from Muscat to Manila nearly hit a Jet Air flight from Bombay to Delhi.
It cited outdated communications equipment used by Indian air traffic controllers.

The pilots' union said a second mid-air collision was averted on January 6, 1995, between a Gulf Air aircraft travelling from Abu Dhabi to Trivandrum in southern India, and an Egypt Air flight from Trivandrum to Muscat.
A third near miss was on April 6, 1995, between an Air France 747 jumbo carrying 395 passengers and an Indian Airlines flight near Delhi airport, it said.
The letter said "the air corridors in the Indian skies are becoming more and more crowded and congested".
The ICPA said the government had failed to equip major airports, including New Delhi, with working state-of-the-art radar equipment, called transponders.
Unlike conventional radar, transponders allow air traffic controllers to keep track of an aircraft's altitude and speed, critical in preventing two planes from colliding.
Ordinary radar shows the plane's direction.
The ICPA had recommended the installation of transponders, very high frequency (VHF) communications equipment and CAT II equipment to aid landings at major airports.
A senior flight safety official at state-owned Indian Airlines said a transponder had been installed at the Delhi airport but was not operational.
"They have been very, very slow in installing a transponder," said a senior ICPA official, who asked not to be identified.
"It would have been better to have a transponder yesterday at Delhi airport," the Indian Airlines safety official said.
"If two aircraft are closing in on each other, it can't be seen on traditional radar," the official added.
Airport Authority officials were not immediately available for comment on the status of the transponder.

A civil aviation ministry spokeswoman had no information on the transponder but said the ministry had formed a committee in September to review aircraft legislation dating from the 1930s, as well as safety regulations.
